screens.title: Navigating the 3D Viewport and Basic Scene Setup
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter teaches the foundational skills that make Houdini practical every day: reliable viewport navigation, a clear scene hierarchy, creating basic geometry, and using transform manipulators. You will learn the three essential camera motions — tumble, pan, and zoom — and the hotkeys that make them fast. We will also open and populate the obj level so you can create geometry by either clicking a shelf tool or by inserting nodes with the Tab menu. Finally, you’ll practice moving, rotating, and scaling objects with manipulators and numeric parameters so your models sit exactly where they should. These are core skills you will repeat in every project. A short example you’ll practice in the hands-on activity is building a tabletop from a box primitive and copying four leg primitives into place, then parenting legs to the tabletop so transforms propagate correctly. A common beginner mistake is losing orientation in the viewport or moving a child without remembering it inherits its parent’s transform; we’ll highlight checks to avoid both. By the end you’ll be faster, more confident, and ready to begin procedural node work.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Overview
Navigating the 3D Viewport and Basic Scene Setup
Build muscle memory for navigation, create primitives, and apply precise transformations.
In this lesson

Learn Alt + mouse navigation, shelf vs Tab creation, manipulators (T, R, E), and scene parenting so your models behave predictably.

Why it matters

Good viewport control and a clean scene graph speed iteration and make exports to game engines consistent in scale and orientation.

Create Geometry

Navigation
Alt + mouse for tumble, pan, zoom.
Primitives

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical, verifiable skills. First, you will master viewport navigation: tumble, pan, and zoom using Alt with mouse buttons and the wheel, and you’ll use frame-all and frame-selection hotkeys to regain orientation. A concrete example is repeatedly framing your tabletop so it sits perfectly in view before moving legs. Second, you will understand the scene hierarchy: how parent and child objects relate and why children inherit parent transforms. This matters when you parent wheels to a car body so all motion stays consistent. Third, you will create primitives using both the Shelf Tools for quick placement and the Tab menu for procedural nodes; you will know when each method is preferable. For example, use Shelf for rapid mockups and Tab inside a geometry node when you need a procedural chain. Fourth, you will apply transformations precisely with manipulators and numeric parameters: translate, rotate, scale and the T, R, E hotkeys. You will be able to position objects to exact coordinates and avoid the common mistake of moving something in world space when you meant local space.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Skill Checklist
Viewport Practice
  • Hold Alt + LMB to tumble around a point until the corner lines up visually.
  • Hold Alt + MMB to pan to align objects without rotating the view.
  • Hold Alt + RMB or use the wheel to zoom smoothly; use Spacebar + G if lost.
Mnemonic: Tumble = rotate, Pan = slide, Zoom = move closer.
Scene Graph & Parenting
  • Drag a child onto a parent in the Scene Graph to establish inheritance.
  • Move the parent to confirm children follow; check local offsets when needed.
  • Avoid moving children expecting global independence once parented.
Verified competency: parent four legs to a tabletop and move the table.
Create Primitives
  • Use Shelf Tools for rapid placement of boxes or spheres at the origin.
  • Use Tab inside a geometry node to create SOPs and see procedural chaining.
  • Prefer Tab when you need node-level control or to expose parameters later.
Transforms & Manipulators
  • Press T to translate, R to rotate, and E to scale and use handles visually.
  • Use Parameter Editor to enter precise numeric values for Translate, Rotate, Scale.
  • Check local vs world space when results seem unexpected.
Tip

If you ever lose orientation, press Spacebar + G to frame all objects and regain a stable view before continuing.

screens.title: Viewport Navigation: Tumble, Pan, Zoom
screens.narratorSegment: Viewport navigation is the simplest skill with the biggest payoff. In Houdini the three essential motions are tumble, pan, and zoom. Tumble rotates the camera around a central point so you can inspect an object from all angles. You perform tumble by holding Alt and the left mouse button while dragging. Pan slides the view horizontally or vertically without rotating; hold Alt and the middle mouse button and drag. Zoom moves the camera closer or further; hold Alt and the right mouse button and drag, or use the mouse wheel for discrete steps. A concrete example: when adjusting one corner of the tabletop, use tumble to find the corner angle, pan to line it up, then zoom in to place the leg precisely. A common misconception is thinking zoom is equivalent to dollying in local camera space; in practice, your zoom can feel different depending on where the current pivot or central point is. Spacebar + F will frame the selected object so tumble rotates around that selection, and Spacebar + G frames the entire scene to recover from disorientation. Practicing these motions together until they feel natural will let you focus on modeling instead of fighting the camera. Now ask yourself: after framing a selection, can you maintain that pivot while tumbling and place a leg without reorienting the view?

keyIdea.title: Essential control
keyIdea.text: Tumble, pan, and zoom using Alt + mouse; use framing hotkeys to set pivots and recover orientation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Viewport Navigation
How it works
  1. Tumble: Alt + LMB. Rotates around the current pivot or framed selection.
  2. Pan: Alt + MMB. Slides view without rotating the camera orientation.
  3. Zoom: Alt + RMB or mouse wheel. Moves camera toward or away from the pivot.
Practice sequence: Frame the tabletop, tumble to a corner, pan to center, zoom to adjust.
Common mistake
Confusing world dolly with pivot zoom; always frame your selection to control the pivot before close inspection.
Pro tip
Use Spacebar + F to temporarily re-center the pivot on a selected object for precise tumbling.
Practice steps
Step 1 — Frame and Tumble
Select a corner of your tabletop, press Spacebar + F, then hold Alt + LMB and rotate around that corner until the angle is clear.
Step 2 — Pan and Zoom
Hold Alt + MMB to slide the view so the corner is centered, then Alt + RMB to zoom close and align the leg origin precisely.
Key Takeaway

Control your pivot with framing hotkeys and use Alt + mouse to inspect and position elements quickly.

screens.title: Creating Primitives: Shelf Tools vs Tab Menu
screens.narratorSegment: Houdini gives you two common ways to create basic geometry: the Shelf Tools and the Tab menu inside the network. Shelf Tools are immediate: click the Box icon on the Create shelf and a box appears at the origin. This is perfect for rapid mockups or when you need to block out a scene quickly. The Tab menu is procedural: at the obj level you press Tab and create a Geometry node, dive inside, press Tab again and type box to add a Box SOP in a node chain. This method is essential when you need to edit parameters later or connect additional operators. A concrete example: use the Shelf to drop a quick tabletop during layout, but use Tab when you want that tabletop to be part of a reusable procedural asset where size, subdivisions, or subsequent modifiers can be adjusted by changing node parameters. A common misconception is that Shelf-created geometry cannot be procedural; it can, but placing it through the shelf often creates objects at the top level that you may need to reorganize into nodes. Decide based on speed versus control, and practice creating the same box both ways to see the difference.

keyIdea.title: Quick vs procedural
keyIdea.text: Shelf is fast for mockups; Tab inside geometry nodes gives procedural flexibility and node-level control.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Create Primitives
Shelf Tools
Immediate placement for boxes, spheres, grids and more. Good for rapid blocking and layout. Objects appear in the scene quickly without you writing node chains.
Pros
  • Speed
  • Convenience
Cons
  • Less immediate procedural chaining
  • May require reorganization into nodes
Example

Drop a Box from the Create shelf to block a tabletop, then later recreate it with Tab inside a geometry node when you need adjustable dimensions.

Tab Menu (Procedural)
Create a Geometry node at the obj level, dive inside, then press Tab and add a Box SOP. This places the primitive in a node network you can extend, parameterize, and reuse as an asset.
Pros
  • Full procedural control
  • Easy parameter exposure
Misconception
Some assume Tab is slower; in reality procedural setup takes a moment but saves time for iterative changes.
Try this

Create the same box with both methods and compare how easy it is to change size later.

screens.title: Transformations: Translate, Rotate, Scale
screens.narratorSegment: Transformations change an object’s position, orientation, or size. Translation moves an object along X, Y, and Z axes. Rotation turns an object around those axes. Scaling changes the dimensions of the object. In Houdini you can perform these with manipulators or by entering numbers in the parameter editor. A concrete workflow: select an object, press T to reveal arrows for translation, drag an arrow to slide along that axis, or type Translate X, Y, Z values to place the object at exact coordinates. Press R to show rotation rings and rotate numerically with degrees in the parameter fields. Press E to reveal scaling handles; uniform and non-uniform scaling are both available. A common beginner mistake is confusing local and world space transforms — rotating in world space may not produce the same visual result as rotating in local object space. If your values seem wrong, check whether you are working in object or local space and whether parent transforms are affecting your object. The best practice is to use manipulators for quick adjustments and parameter fields for repeatable precision. After this, try setting Translate X to a specific value and verify the object moved exactly as expected.

keyIdea.title: Transform fundamentals
keyIdea.text: Use manipulators for speed and parameter fields for precision; always be aware of local vs world space and parent transforms.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Transformations
What each transform does
  • Translate moves an object along X, Y, Z coordinates; use T or numeric Translate fields.
  • Rotate orients an object around axes; use R or numeric Rotate fields.
  • Scale resizes an object uniformly or non-uniformly; use E or Scale parameters.
Common mistake
Applying transforms without checking parent influence. A child inherits parent transforms and may appear to snap when the parent moves.
Concrete example
Create a box sized for a tabletop, set Translate Y so it rests on the ground plane, then rotate the tabletop 5 degrees around Z to test orientation. Finally scale uniformly to adjust overall size. Use parameter fields to type exact values for reproducible results.
Key Takeaway

Combine manipulators for quick edits and numeric parameters for exact placement; always verify local vs world orientation and parent influence.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build a Tabletop Scene
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on sequence guides you through a short exercise that reinforces navigation, primitive creation, transforms, and parenting. Start a new scene. At the obj level, create a Geometry node and name it tabletop_geo. Dive inside and add a Box SOP. Set Size to two by point one by one comma five — in practice enter Size 2, 0.1, 1.5 — and set Center Y to 0.05 so the bottom rests on the ground plane. Exit to the obj level and make another Geometry node leg_geo. Inside leg_geo create a Box SOP sized 0.1, 1, 0.1 with Center Y at 0.5 so it sits on the ground. Use T to translate the leg to one corner using Translate X and Z values like 0.9 and 0.6. Duplicate the leg three times, place them at the four corners by changing Translate values, and verify alignment with tumble and pan. Finally, open the Scene Graph, drag each leg onto the tabletop object to parent them. Test parenting by moving or rotating the tabletop and observing that legs follow. A common oversight is forgetting to set Center Y so geometry appears intersecting the ground; correct centers first then position.

keyIdea.title: Practice result
keyIdea.text: A tabletop object with four parented legs, positioned and verified using navigation and transform skills.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step
  1. File → New to start a fresh scene.
  2. At obj level create Geometry node named tabletop_geo; dive inside and add Box SOP.
  3. Set Box Size to 2, 0.1, 1.5 and Center Y to 0.05 so it rests on ground.
  4. Create leg_geo with a Box SOP sized 0.1, 1, 0.1 and Center Y 0.5; translate to a corner using T or numeric values.
  5. Duplicate leg_geo three times, move duplicates to remaining corners using Translate X/Z values.
  6. In Scene Graph parent each leg to the tabletop so transforms propagate.
Checklist & Tips
  • Verify Center Y on boxes to avoid clipping through ground.
  • Use Spacebar + F to focus on a leg, then Alt + LMB to fine-tune orientation.
  • After parenting, move the tabletop to confirm legs inherit transforms.
Key Takeaway

Follow procedural creation steps and always verify center and parenting to prevent alignment surprises.

screens.title: Scene Hierarchy and the Scene Graph
screens.narratorSegment: Scene hierarchy is the tree of objects that organizes your scene. The Scene Graph displays this tree and lets you create parent-child relationships by dragging one object onto another. The key behavioral rule is inheritance: children inherit the parent’s transformations. For a concrete example imagine a car object with wheel children. If you move or rotate the car, wheels move and rotate with it, preserving local offsets. A frequent beginner confusion is attempting to move a child independently after parented and seeing it snap or appear to maintain a position relative to the world. Remember that children are positioned relative to their parent’s coordinate space. If you must adjust a child without inheriting, temporarily unparent it or edit local transforms while accounting for the parent’s current transform. For game assets, consistent scaling convention helps — many teams treat one Houdini unit as one meter. This consistency prevents scale drift when exporting to engines, and it makes collision sizes and animation rigs predictable. A useful check is to move the parent and watch children to confirm you understand how transforms cascade.

keyIdea.title: Hierarchy rule
keyIdea.text: Children inherit parent transforms; organize assets so related parts move together and verify local vs world offsets when adjusting children.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Scene Hierarchy
What the Scene Graph shows
A tree of objects where parent nodes contain child nodes. Parent transforms automatically affect children. Use drag-and-drop in the Scene Graph to create relationships.
Concrete example
Make a Car parent and Wheel children. Translate the car and watch wheels follow. Rotate the car and the wheels inherit that rotation while keeping local offsets.
Pitfall
Attempting to move a child without unparenting will apply a local offset relative to the parent’s space — the result may not match expectations if you think in world coordinates.
Practical guidelines
  • Group related parts under a single parent to move them together.
  • Use parenting for animation rigs and modular assets so transforms propagate predictably.
  • Keep scale conventions consistent; treat 1 unit as 1 meter for game exports when required.
Key Takeaway

Use the Scene Graph intentionally to organize assets; check parent influence before making local edits to children.

screens.title: Manipulators: Visual Handles and Planar Movement
screens.narratorSegment: Manipulators are the visual handles that let you edit transforms directly in the viewport. When you press T you reveal axis arrows for translate: drag an arrow to move along a single axis, or drag the square between two arrows to move on a plane such as XY or XZ. Press R to reveal rotation rings around each axis; drag a ring to rotate around that axis. Press E to reveal scale boxes; grab a corner to scale on multiple axes or use the center handle for uniform scale. An example workflow: select a leg, press T, drag the X arrow to place it at Translate X 0.9, then press R to rotate the leg slightly so it lines up with tabletop chamfering. A common misconception is to assume plane drags always move in world-aligned planes — plane movement respects the manipulator orientation which can be affected by object local axes or parent transforms. If a handle behaves unexpectedly, check whether the manipulator is in local or world mode and whether the parent transform rotates the local axes. Manipulators speed layout but require awareness of coordinate spaces to avoid surprises. Try switching manipulator modes and observe the difference to internalize the distinction.

keyIdea.title: Manipulators in practice
keyIdea.text: Axis arrows, plane squares, and rings let you move, constrain, and rotate precisely; confirm local vs world mode when results differ from expectations.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Manipulators
Handle types
  • Axis arrows: constrain movement to a single axis.
  • Plane squares: move along two axes simultaneously (XY, XZ, YZ).
  • Rotation rings: rotate around the chosen axis smoothly.
Example
Use the plane square between X and Z to slide the leg along the tabletop plane without changing height.
Mode awareness
Manipulators can operate in local or world space. Local mode aligns handles to the object's orientation, which may be rotated by a parent. World mode locks to scene axes. If movement behaves unexpectedly, check the manipulator mode and parent transforms.
Practice switching between T, R, and E while observing axis alignment and plane behavior. This will build an intuitive sense of when to use plane drags versus axis locks for precise placement.
Key Takeaway

Manipulators are fast and visual, but always confirm coordinate space and parent rotation to avoid unintended offsets.

screens.title: Framing and Pivot: Spacebar Shortcuts
screens.narratorSegment: Framing shortcuts give you control over the camera pivot and quickly reorient your view. Spacebar + F frames the selected object, which also sets the pivot used by tumble and zoom. Spacebar + G frames all objects in the scene, serving as a quick reset when you feel lost. A typical usage: select a leg, press Spacebar + F, then tumble to rotate around that leg and place it exactly where you want. If you skip framing, tumble may rotate around a distant or unintended pivot and make exact placement difficult. Beginners often overuse arbitrary manual adjustments and then cannot reproduce camera positions; framing makes the process repeatable. Another subtle point: framing a selection does not change object transforms — it only moves the camera and pivot. This means you can safely frame and then test manipulators without altering your geometry. Practice: select each leg and press Spacebar + F, tumble and pan to align it, then press Spacebar + G to view the full table. Can you reliably return to the same pivot after moving the camera? Framing and Pivot: Spacebar Shortcuts means use spacebar + f to set the pivot to a selection and spacebar + g to frame everything; framing is a viewport action and does not change object transforms.. In practical terms, use framing hotkeys to control pivot and recover view orientation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

fullNarratorScript:
This chapter teaches the foundational skills that make Houdini practical every day: reliable viewport navigation, a clear scene hierarchy, creating basic geometry, and using transform manipulators. You will learn the three essential camera motions — tumble, pan, and zoom — and the hotkeys that make them fast. We will also open and populate the obj level so you can create geometry by either clicking a shelf tool or by inserting nodes with the Tab menu. Finally, you’ll practice moving, rotating, and scaling objects with manipulators and numeric parameters so your models sit exactly where they should. These are core skills you will repeat in every project. A short example you’ll practice in the hands-on activity is building a tabletop from a box primitive and copying four leg primitives into place, then parenting legs to the tabletop so transforms propagate correctly. A common beginner mistake is losing orientation in the viewport or moving a child without remembering it inherits its parent’s transform; we’ll highlight checks to avoid both. By the end you’ll be faster, more confident, and ready to begin procedural node work.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical, verifiable skills. First, you will master viewport navigation: tumble, pan, and zoom using Alt with mouse buttons and the wheel, and you’ll use frame-all and frame-selection hotkeys to regain orientation. A concrete example is repeatedly framing your tabletop so it sits perfectly in view before moving legs. Second, you will understand the scene hierarchy: how parent and child objects relate and why children inherit parent transforms. This matters when you parent wheels to a car body so all motion stays consistent. Third, you will create primitives using both the Shelf Tools for quick placement and the Tab menu for procedural nodes; you will know when each method is preferable. For example, use Shelf for rapid mockups and Tab inside a geometry node when you need a procedural chain. Fourth, you will apply transformations precisely with manipulators and numeric parameters: translate, rotate, scale and the T, R, E hotkeys. You will be able to position objects to exact coordinates and avoid the common mistake of moving something in world space when you meant local space.

This slide breaks each objective into measurable steps you can practice now. For viewport navigation, practice holding Alt with each mouse button and the wheel, and use Spacebar + F and Spacebar + G to frame selections and the whole scene. A good verification is to center and frame your tabletop and then tumble around a fixed corner. For scene hierarchy, practice parenting legs to a tabletop in the Scene Graph and then move the parent to confirm children follow. Watch for the common trap where you try to move a child and forget it remains offset in parent space. For creating primitives, alternate between the Shelf and the Tab menu: place a box with the Create shelf and then recreate it procedurally inside a geometry node to see the difference in flexibility. For transforms, switch between manipulators and numeric fields: use T, R, and E and then set Translate and Rotate values in the parameter editor to exact numbers. These steps make each objective verifiable and reproducible.

Viewport navigation is the simplest skill with the biggest payoff. In Houdini the three essential motions are tumble, pan, and zoom. Tumble rotates the camera around a central point so you can inspect an object from all angles. You perform tumble by holding Alt and the left mouse button while dragging. Pan slides the view horizontally or vertically without rotating; hold Alt and the middle mouse button and drag. Zoom moves the camera closer or further; hold Alt and the right mouse button and drag, or use the mouse wheel for discrete steps. A concrete example: when adjusting one corner of the tabletop, use tumble to find the corner angle, pan to line it up, then zoom in to place the leg precisely. A common misconception is thinking zoom is equivalent to dollying in local camera space; in practice, your zoom can feel different depending on where the current pivot or central point is. Spacebar + F will frame the selected object so tumble rotates around that selection, and Spacebar + G frames the entire scene to recover from disorientation. Practicing these motions together until they feel natural will let you focus on modeling instead of fighting the camera. Now ask yourself: after framing a selection, can you maintain that pivot while tumbling and place a leg without reorienting the view?

Houdini gives you two common ways to create basic geometry: the Shelf Tools and the Tab menu inside the network. Shelf Tools are immediate: click the Box icon on the Create shelf and a box appears at the origin. This is perfect for rapid mockups or when you need to block out a scene quickly. The Tab menu is procedural: at the obj level you press Tab and create a Geometry node, dive inside, press Tab again and type box to add a Box SOP in a node chain. This method is essential when you need to edit parameters later or connect additional operators. A concrete example: use the Shelf to drop a quick tabletop during layout, but use Tab when you want that tabletop to be part of a reusable procedural asset where size, subdivisions, or subsequent modifiers can be adjusted by changing node parameters. A common misconception is that Shelf-created geometry cannot be procedural; it can, but placing it through the shelf often creates objects at the top level that you may need to reorganize into nodes. Decide based on speed versus control, and practice creating the same box both ways to see the difference.

Transformations change an object’s position, orientation, or size. Translation moves an object along X, Y, and Z axes. Rotation turns an object around those axes. Scaling changes the dimensions of the object. In Houdini you can perform these with manipulators or by entering numbers in the parameter editor. A concrete workflow: select an object, press T to reveal arrows for translation, drag an arrow to slide along that axis, or type Translate X, Y, Z values to place the object at exact coordinates. Press R to show rotation rings and rotate numerically with degrees in the parameter fields. Press E to reveal scaling handles; uniform and non-uniform scaling are both available. A common beginner mistake is confusing local and world space transforms — rotating in world space may not produce the same visual result as rotating in local object space. If your values seem wrong, check whether you are working in object or local space and whether parent transforms are affecting your object. The best practice is to use manipulators for quick adjustments and parameter fields for repeatable precision. After this, try setting Translate X to a specific value and verify the object moved exactly as expected.

This hands-on sequence guides you through a short exercise that reinforces navigation, primitive creation, transforms, and parenting. Start a new scene. At the obj level, create a Geometry node and name it tabletop_geo. Dive inside and add a Box SOP. Set Size to two by point one by one comma five — in practice enter Size 2, 0.1, 1.5 — and set Center Y to 0.05 so the bottom rests on the ground plane. Exit to the obj level and make another Geometry node leg_geo. Inside leg_geo create a Box SOP sized 0.1, 1, 0.1 with Center Y at 0.5 so it sits on the ground. Use T to translate the leg to one corner using Translate X and Z values like 0.9 and 0.6. Duplicate the leg three times, place them at the four corners by changing Translate values, and verify alignment with tumble and pan. Finally, open the Scene Graph, drag each leg onto the tabletop object to parent them. Test parenting by moving or rotating the tabletop and observing that legs follow. A common oversight is forgetting to set Center Y so geometry appears intersecting the ground; correct centers first then position.

Scene hierarchy is the tree of objects that organizes your scene. The Scene Graph displays this tree and lets you create parent-child relationships by dragging one object onto another. The key behavioral rule is inheritance: children inherit the parent’s transformations. For a concrete example imagine a car object with wheel children. If you move or rotate the car, wheels move and rotate with it, preserving local offsets. A frequent beginner confusion is attempting to move a child independently after parented and seeing it snap or appear to maintain a position relative to the world. Remember that children are positioned relative to their parent’s coordinate space. If you must adjust a child without inheriting, temporarily unparent it or edit local transforms while accounting for the parent’s current transform. For game assets, consistent scaling convention helps — many teams treat one Houdini unit as one meter. This consistency prevents scale drift when exporting to engines, and it makes collision sizes and animation rigs predictable. A useful check is to move the parent and watch children to confirm you understand how transforms cascade.

Manipulators are the visual handles that let you edit transforms directly in the viewport. When you press T you reveal axis arrows for translate: drag an arrow to move along a single axis, or drag the square between two arrows to move on a plane such as XY or XZ. Press R to reveal rotation rings around each axis; drag a ring to rotate around that axis. Press E to reveal scale boxes; grab a corner to scale on multiple axes or use the center handle for uniform scale. An example workflow: select a leg, press T, drag the X arrow to place it at Translate X 0.9, then press R to rotate the leg slightly so it lines up with tabletop chamfering. A common misconception is to assume plane drags always move in world-aligned planes — plane movement respects the manipulator orientation which can be affected by object local axes or parent transforms. If a handle behaves unexpectedly, check whether the manipulator is in local or world mode and whether the parent transform rotates the local axes. Manipulators speed layout but require awareness of coordinate spaces to avoid surprises. Try switching manipulator modes and observe the difference to internalize the distinction.

Framing shortcuts give you control over the camera pivot and quickly reorient your view. Spacebar + F frames the selected object, which also sets the pivot used by tumble and zoom. Spacebar + G frames all objects in the scene, serving as a quick reset when you feel lost. A typical usage: select a leg, press Spacebar + F, then tumble to rotate around that leg and place it exactly where you want. If you skip framing, tumble may rotate around a distant or unintended pivot and make exact placement difficult.
